results.title: Anthropic disrupts bioweapons research efforts, Russian hacking, Chinese Claude misuse
results.author: By AJ Vicens and Eduardo Baptista
results.content:
By AJ Vicens and Eduardo Baptista
Sept 10 (Reuters) - Anthropic broke up attempts to use its Claude models to develop biological weapons and carry out a suspected Russia-linked cyber espionage campaign against Ukraine, the AI heavyweight said in a report published on Thursday.
It also accused Chinese competitors of hacking attempts aimed at extracting Claude's capabilities in its latest Threat Intelligence report, which documented malicious use of its technology over the past eight months.
A growing number of illegal hacking attempts by rogue AI agents along with concerns over the technology's risks voiced by industry insiders have increased the pressure on leading pioneers in the field, raising the prospect of more regulation.
Two Anthropic researchers warned this week that rapidly progressing artificial intelligence could lead to the extinction of the human race in the not-too-distant future.
MISSILES, DRONES AND BIOLOGICAL WEAPONS
In its report, Anthropic said it has long been a concern that AI models might one day reach the level of capability where they could help make existing pathogens more dangerous or create entirely new ones.
It documented five examples of scientists using its models in ways that could support biological weapons development.
In one case, a researcher in a region unsupported by Anthropic employed virtual private server infrastructure to access Claude and for weeks used it to plan avian influenza mammalian-adaptation experiments.
Regions not supported by Anthropic include countries like Russia, China and North Korea among others.
After detecting the misuse, it banned the accounts involved in such research and incorporated its findings into its frontier model safeguards, enforcement, and threat intelligence processes.
Anthropic did not identify the institutions, the countries where they are based, or the specific biological agents and research techniques involved.
It also identified what it called "new categories of threat actors" misusing Claude. That included using the platform to "develop software for conventional weapons, including firearms, missiles, armed drones, bombs, and other munitions, as well as the targeting and control systems that operate them."
The report detailed incidents of operators in China, Russia and Yemen using Claude to develop software for weapons design and development, or to support intelligence gathering and procurement related to weapons programs.
Rapid improvements in Anthropic's models have raised new risks, Jacob Klein, its head of threat intelligence, told Reuters.
results.summary:
Anthropic successfully blocked attempts to use its Claude artificial intelligence models for biological weapons development and cyber espionage campaigns linked to actors in Russia and China.

### Key Points
- Anthropic identified five instances where users attempted to leverage its AI models to facilitate the development of dangerous biological pathogens.
- The company detected and blocked efforts by operators in Russia, China, and Yemen to use Claude for designing conventional weapons and targeting systems.
- A suspected Russia-linked cyber espionage campaign targeting Ukraine was thwarted after the company identified and banned the accounts involved.
- Anthropic reported that Chinese competitors have attempted to hack its systems to extract proprietary capabilities from its frontier AI models.
- The company has updated its safety protocols and enforcement processes to address these emerging threats from rogue AI agents.

### Why it Matters
These findings highlight the escalating security risks associated with increasingly powerful generative AI models as they become targets for state-sponsored espionage and weapons development. The report underscores the urgent need for robust safety guardrails and regulatory oversight to prevent advanced technology from being weaponized by malicious actors.

results.title: Apple Explains What Happens to Conversations Siri Recap Hears
results.author: Juli Clover
results.content:
The Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4 have new Audio Intelligence features that include Sound Recognition, Music Recognition, Live Rewind, and Siri Recap. When these features are activated, the new Apple Watches are always listening to what's going on around the wearer.
With Siri Recap, the Apple Watch listens to your conversations throughout the day and takes notes. It uses Apple Intelligence to continually generate summaries that Apple says are meant to "jog your memory" on events so you can stay present in the moment.
Apple anticipated negative reactions to a wearable that's always listening, so it has a detailed explainer on the privacy features that have been added.
- No speaker attribution - Siri Recap will not identify and attribute speakers. Names can be included if mentioned in the conversation, but nothing is directly attributed to a specific person.
- Omitted information - Siri Recaps will omit potentially harmful content or sensitive data, which Apple says includes language that promotes self-harm or hateful speech, financial data, government-assigned identifiers, authentication data, and certain personal identifiers.
- Caveats - Apple warns that Siri Recap summaries can be incomplete or inaccurate, and filtering may not remove all sensitive information.
- No transcript - Apple says Siri Recap doesn't produce a full transcript of a conversation. It's just a summary, comparable to notes one might jot down after a conversation.
- Condensed conversations - Encrypted, condensed text versions of a conversation are sent to Private Cloud Compute. The text is less than half the length of the original transcript, and distills the conversation to its core meaning. Conversation tone, non-essential language, filler words, and redundancies are removed.
- No audio recording - Audio is sent to the Secure Exclave on Apple Watch and iPhone for processing and analysis. It can't be accessed by the operating system, apps, the user, or Apple, and no audio is recorded or stored.
- Private Cloud Compute - Siri Recap uses Apple Foundation Models running on Private Cloud Compute to summarize and format the final output. Data is not accessible to Apple or anyone else.
- Opt in, not opt out - Siri Recap can be turned on in the Apple Watch app on iPhone, and set to listen on a schedule. You can have it on only at work, or set it to never listen at night. There will be a quick access toggle in Control Center for turning it on and off.
- Auto-delete - Summaries auto-delete after seven days if not saved to the Siri app.
- Siri app - Summaries are saved to the Siri app and can be deleted at any time from all synced devices. Saved summaries can be exported to other apps like Notes.
- Encryption - Summaries are end-to-end encrypted when synced to your other devices via iCloud so only your trusted devices can access them.
Apple suggests that Apple Watch wearers "be mindful" of the people around them. "While audio is not recorded and stored, and no speakers are attributed, consider those around you where conversations might be private or sensitive," reads Apple's document.
Siri Recap requires one of the new Apple Watch models and an iPhone 16 or later (except the iPhone 16e). The feature is launching later this year.
results.summary:
Apple is introducing new Audio Intelligence features, including the Siri Recap note-taking tool, for the upcoming Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4 models launching later this year.

### Key Points
- Siri Recap uses Apple Intelligence to generate conversation summaries, omitting sensitive data like financial information and government identifiers.
- The feature processes audio locally on the device's Secure Exclave and sends condensed, encrypted text to Private Cloud Compute for analysis.
- Apple confirms that no full audio recordings are stored, speaker attribution is disabled, and summaries automatically delete after seven days.
- Users must manually opt in to the feature and can manage scheduling or toggle recording via the Apple Watch app and Control Center.
- The functionality requires an Apple Watch Series 12 or Ultra 4 paired with an iPhone 16 or later, excluding the iPhone 16e model.

### Why it Matters
This update represents a significant shift in wearable technology by integrating continuous ambient listening to assist with memory and productivity. While Apple emphasizes privacy through encryption and local processing, the feature raises new social and ethical considerations regarding consent in public or private spaces.

results.title: Storage infrastructure will underpin post-quantum security
results.author: Uwe Kemmer
results.content:
AI has rewritten the enterprise data playbook. Workflows no longer just create temporary operational data, but vast amounts of high-value assets, from LLM training datasets and model outputs to logs, metadata and archived knowledge that may need to be preserved for years.
Director of EMEAI Field Engineering at WD (Western Digital).
As enterprise tech leaders seek to scale infrastructure to meet these demands, storage requirements are undergoing a fundamental shift. Capacity and performance remain critical, but data security has become equally important. Today, long-term data integrity and absolute cyber resilience carry equal weight.
Protecting this data, however, is no longer just about defeating today’s threat vectors. It requires preparing storage infrastructure for a significant shift: the arrival of quantum computing.
Data is a long-term strategic asset, not a short-lived trend
AI is accelerating data growth, but it can also extend the useful life of information. Data recorded today will be harvested for compliance, advanced analytics and model retraining for years to come.
To manage this economically, enterprise architectures rely heavily on high-capacity HDDs. While flash technologies dominate performance-critical hot tiers, HDDs remain the undisputed backbone of large-scale storage, providing the capacity, economics and longevity needed to archive data at scale.
As a result, organizations must consider how to protect not only today's data, but also its future value. After all, if the underlying infrastructure is compromised down the road, the very assets driving future AI innovations become the biggest operational and regulatory liability.
Harvest now, decrypt later
Current encryption technologies remain effective against conventional threats. However, quantum computing is expected to challenge some of the cryptographic methods used for authentication and key exchange.

This has led to concerns around “harvest now, decrypt later” attacks, where encrypted data is collected today with the expectation that future quantum capabilities could potentially decrypt it later.
For organizations storing sensitive intellectual property, research data or AI training datasets, this means security decisions made today could have implications for years to come.
Preparing for that future requires action from security leaders and IT directors now.
Security must be built into the infrastructure
Security is often viewed through the lens of data encryption, and with good reason. Self-encrypting drives (SEDs) provide always-on, hardware-based AES-256 encryption that helps protect data at rest without impacting performance.
But protecting data alone is no longer enough.
Storage devices themselves must be trusted. Firmware, authentication mechanisms, provisioning processes and diagnostic tools all play a role in ensuring a drive operates securely throughout its lifecycle.
If attackers compromise a device's firmware or trust architecture, broader security controls can be undermined regardless of how data is encrypted elsewhere in the system. This makes storage security a critical component of overall cyber resilience.
Implementing quantum-resistant defenses in storage
To counter these emerging attack vectors, the storage industry is actively embedding post-quantum cryptography into hardware architecture of enterprise hard drives. Rather than focusing solely on protecting data, the objective is to protect the trust architecture that underpins the drive itself.
Post quantum cryptography (PQC) technologies are being incorporated into areas such as secure key establishment, firmware authentication, secure provisioning, and trusted diagnostics. These capabilities are designed in alignment with established NIST post-quantum standards and are implemented using hybrid approaches that combine classical cryptography with quantum-resistant algorithms.
In practical terms, this means that the mechanisms responsible for establishing trust, validating firmware integrity and protecting administrative functions can remain resilient against both conventional and future quantum-enabled attacks. With the operational service life of HDDs often spanning 5 years (or more), implementing PQC today helps protect against quantum-based threats that may not materialize for several years, but that we know are coming.
Importantly, HDDs have long incorporated security controls to defend against today's threats. PQC does not replace these protections; it enhances them by adding an additional layer of resilience against emerging attack vectors.
Trust in the AI era
For many years, storage innovation was primarily defined by increases in capacity. Today, the expectations placed on infrastructure are much broader.
Organizations seek storage platforms that can scale with AI-driven data growth, deliver reliable performance, preserve integrity over long retention periods and withstand an increasingly complex threat environment.
PQC represents an important step in that evolution. By extending protection beyond data encryption and into the trust mechanisms that underpin storage devices themselves, PQC-enabled HDDs help organizations prepare for the security challenges of tomorrow while protecting the data they manage today.
As AI continues to elevate the strategic value of enterprise data, security can no longer be a short-term, reactive consideration. Trust must be engineered directly into the hardware layer and built to outlast the threats of today, tomorrow and the quantum era ahead of us.

Western Digital is integrating post-quantum cryptography into enterprise hard drives to protect long-term data assets against future quantum computing threats and evolving cyber security risks in AI workflows.

### Key Points
- Enterprise data growth driven by AI requires long-term storage solutions that prioritize both massive capacity and advanced cyber resilience.
- The "harvest now, decrypt later" threat model involves attackers collecting encrypted data today to decrypt it once quantum computing capabilities mature.
- Western Digital is embedding post-quantum cryptography (PQC) into hardware to secure firmware authentication, key establishment, and diagnostic tools.
- New PQC implementations align with NIST standards, utilizing hybrid approaches that combine classical encryption with quantum-resistant algorithms.
- Hard drives are being engineered to maintain trust architectures throughout their five-year operational lifecycles, protecting data against both current and future threats.

### Why it Matters
As AI transforms data into a long-term strategic asset, organizations must ensure their storage infrastructure remains secure against future technological shifts. Integrating quantum-resistant defenses at the hardware level prevents sensitive intellectual property from becoming a long-term regulatory or operational liability.

results.title: Solana’s Apps Lost Half Their Value and Its ETFs Have Slowed. Which Number Is Right?
results.author: Sam Daodu
results.content:
Solana’s Apps Lost Half Their Value and Its ETFs Have Slowed. Which Number Is Right?
Solana's app ecosystem has shed enormous value while its spot ETFs keep pulling in fresh capital, and both signals are pointing in completely different directions. Figuring out which one actually predicts where SOL goes next changes everything about how you…
The value of many Solana (CRYPTO:SOL) applications and tokens built on the network has fallen sharply, with some parts of the ecosystem losing roughly half their value from earlier highs. At the same time, Solana’s U.S. spot ETFs have continued to attract money overall, although inflows have slowed sharply in recent weeks.
One number points to weaker activity and lower valuations, while the other suggests investors still want exposure to SOL. So, which signal tells us more about where Solana is heading?
Why Have Solana’s Apps Lost Half Their Value?
Solana-based apps and tokens losing roughly 50% does not mean every project on the network has lost half its value. The biggest losses have been concentrated among speculative projects, particularly memecoin-related tokens, launchpads, trading applications and smaller assets whose valuations rose rapidly during periods of heavy retail activity. These projects can lose value much faster than the underlying blockchain when speculation cools.
Solana’s application fees fell 31% quarter over quarter in the second quarter of 2026 to about $552 million. Pump, the leading memecoin launchpad, accounted for $212 million of those fees, or roughly 38% of application fees excluding MEV and staking revenue. Total application revenue fell 55% from the previous quarter to about $198.6 million, while network revenue declined 43% to $51 million.
Those figures show that the slowdown is not purely a valuation issue. Some businesses built on Solana are generating less economic activity than they were during the previous peak. DEX spot trading volume also fell 44% quarter over quarter to $160.8 billion in Q2. Compared with a year earlier, application revenue was down 78%, while network revenue was down 81%.
Regardless, Solana has continued to enjoy meaningful activity. Stablecoin supply increased 48% year over year to $16.3 billion in Q2, while tokenized equity trading reached $8.8 billion, up from $2.1 billion in Q1. Those numbers suggest some activity is shifting away from memecoin speculation toward financial applications and other forms of blockchain use.
That distinction is important because an app token losing 50% does not mean Solana has lost 50% of its users or value. An individual token reflects what investors are willing to pay for that particular project, while SOL reflects the value of the broader network and its future use. Solana can therefore experience a sharp repricing across speculative applications while maintaining significant transaction activity and stablecoin liquidity.
What Does the Weakness in Solana ETFs Tell Us About Demand for SOL?
According to SoSoValue, U.S. spot Solana ETFs have attracted more than $1.3 billion in cumulative net inflows since their October 2025 launch. Solana ETF inflows slowed sharply in early September, with the products recording about $5.25 million in net inflows across the four trading days from September 1 to September 4. That was a major slowdown from the stronger daily flows seen in late August, including $60.91 million on August 27 and $18.08 million on August 28.
ETF flows give investors a regulated way to gain SOL exposure without directly holding the cryptocurrency, which is why they’re a useful gauge of institutional demand. Strong inflows can show that institutional and professional investors are willing to allocate capital to Solana even when the wider crypto market is volatile. Weak flows can indicate that demand is cooling, but weak flows only confirm cooling demand once they persist for several months
For now, the ETF data looks more like a slowdown than a clear institutional exit. That doesn’t guarantee stronger SOL prices, but it shows demand for SOL through ETFs holding up so far, even as app valuations weaken.
Which Number Should Investors Pay More Attention To?
The 50% decline in app valuations and weaker ETF flows answer different questions. App valuations show how investors value individual projects operating on Solana. ETF flows show whether investors want exposure to SOL itself. For someone trying to understand the direction of SOL, ETF flows are therefore the more direct signal.
Application revenue, DEX volume and network fees have all fallen from their earlier peaks, showing that Solana has lost some of the activity that previously supported its ecosystem. A network cannot maintain high valuations indefinitely if users and applications stop generating meaningful economic activity.
However, if ETF inflows remain positive while stablecoin activity, tokenized assets and other network metrics continue growing, the decline in speculative app valuations may prove to be a repricing of weaker projects. If ETF flows turn negative for several months while application revenue, DEX volume and liquidity keep falling, that combination would be the clearer sign that demand for SOL itself is weakening.

results.summary:
Solana is experiencing a divergence as speculative application valuations drop by half while spot ETFs continue to attract institutional capital despite a recent slowdown in net inflows.

### Key Points
- Solana-based application revenue fell 55% quarter-over-quarter in Q2 2026, while network revenue declined by 43%.
- DEX spot trading volume on the network dropped 44% to $160.8 billion during the second quarter.
- Stablecoin supply on Solana grew 48% year-over-year to $16.3 billion, signaling a shift toward financial applications.
- U.S. spot Solana ETFs have accumulated over $1.3 billion in net inflows since their October 2025 launch.
- Daily ETF inflows slowed significantly in early September, recording only $5.25 million over a four-day period.

### Why it Matters
The contrast between falling app valuations and persistent ETF inflows highlights a shift from speculative memecoin trading toward institutional interest in the underlying network. Investors must monitor whether these ETF flows remain positive to determine if the current ecosystem decline is a temporary repricing or a broader loss of demand for SOL.

results.title: From DOGE to space lasers, Alex Gibney peels back the many layers of Elon Musk
results.author: Bobby Allyn
results.content:
From DOGE to "space lasers," Alex Gibney peels back the many layers of Elon Musk
Tesla co-founder Martin Eberhard remembers having dinner with Elon Musk in the early 2000s, when the billionaire became a key investor in the fledgling electric car company. Musk uttered words that Eberhard would never forget: "One thing that nobody can take away from you is that you're the founder of Tesla."
It left a real mark on Eberhard's mind, since Musk would later take unconditional credit for Tesla's runaway success and anoint himself its sole founder, setting off litigation and an eventual settlement that allowed Eberhard and Musk, along with three others, to all claim the title of co-founders of Tesla Motors.
Director Alex Gibney believes those remarks provide a glimpse into who Musk really is: A confidence man who will deceive, gaslight and fabricate to get what he wants.
Eberhard is one of many people who fell in and out of Musk's world who are featured in Gibney's new documentary, Musk, which never drags despite its three hour and 45 minute runtime (which includes a 10-minute intermission). It opens in theaters on October 16.
The film traces Musk's path from his early days as a dot-com-era entrepreneur in Silicon Valley to the present, as one of the world's wealthiest people, exerting extraordinary influence over politics and culture around the world. While many people may be familiar with the general outlines of Musk's story, Gibney taps pivotal characters at crucial moments for the tech mogul to infuse this biography with new life.
Along the way, the Oscar-winning filmmaker, whose past documentaries have taken on corporate greed and government malfeasance, explores Musk's many bitter feuds and contradictions. Gibney attempts to explain how Musk is seen as both a once-in-generational business genius and an impulsive and deranged chaos agent.
I've covered Musk for years, and have been the target of his attacks, so I was initially interested in whether Gibney would dredge up any new revelations, or connect the dots in ways obscured by the steady stream of news about Musk and his many ventures.
While there were very few nuggets of new information, the sheer breadth of the film makes for a stunningly comprehensive accounting of a man Gibney considers a danger to society. We hear from Musk's father, Errol, reflecting on how his son was bullied as a child, there are interviews with Musk's scorned exes, including his first wife, Justine Musk, prying journalists and former business associates who once occupied his orbit.
Early in the film, a far younger Musk is seen on a television program declaring his three animating principles as developing the internet, transitioning the economy to sustainable energy and exploring space. That trio of objectives has remained remarkably consistent for someone whose views and business goals seem to be in a perpetual state of flux.
Gibney first began the project in 2023, thinking it would be a tighter and more focused look at the tech titan. But then Musk barreled his way into Donald Trump's sphere during the 2024 campaign and soon entered the White House, taking a wrecking ball to swaths of the federal government through his cost-cutting effort, DOGE. It led to some observers describing Musk as the "shadow vice president." So Gibney retooled the film as a more ambitious and much longer project to convey just how many facets of modern life are being influenced by one man.
"Particuarly in this bewildering world of inputs that we all live in," Gibney said at a news conference at the Venice Film Festival, where the documentary premiered on Tuesday, "a lot of incidents happen, and there are so many trees, but sometimes it's useful to stitch together a narrative that shows the forest."
Gibney saw parallels between Musk and his past film subjects, including his documentary on the Enron scandal, Enron: The Smartest Guys in the Room, and the downfall of the Silicon Valley blood-testing startup executive Elizabeth Holmes in The Inventor: Out for Blood in Silicon Valley.
"The story of Musk was not in a way a new tech story," Gibney said in Venice. "His story is the story of old wine in a new bottle. His story turns out to be the story of the confidence man, the stock pumper, his wealth and power comes from inflated stock."
Musk did not agree to be interviewed by Gibney, so the filmmaker dove into the archives. (Musk's lawyer claimed in a letter to the film's production company that Gibney "refused" to fact-check the documentary with Musk's team, saying Gibney defamed the billionaire. Musk accused Gibney on X of "fabricating a false film.")
Without Musk's participation, Gibney made a risky choice when it came time to address the many claims and allegations leveled by the billionaire's former exes and business partners: He uses a creepy AI-generated avatar of Musk talking directly to the camera. It's impossible to get used to it.
Appearing svelte and wearing a black leather jacket, AI Musk sits in a gaming chair in front of red and blue lights and echoes words actually spoken by him in podcast appearances and speeches.
Gibney has described his use of AI as "intentionally ironic," but for a project that tackles all the big weighty subjects of our time, the deepfake Musk only serves to cheapen and distract an otherwise serious film.
I felt similarly about other stunts that Gibney deploys. Near the end of the film, Gibney decides to ask Musk's AI tool, Grok, whether robots will save us, an avoidable ask-the-chatbot cliché that doesn't add much.
There are also scenes that transform the film into a first-person- shooter-style video game, including one with a chainsaw-wielding Musk slicing up federal agencies, a far too on-the-nose reference to DOGE that takes the film's narrative off course.
In defending these choices, Gibney wrote in a director's statement handed out to press at a recent screening in Los Angeles that his aim was to subvert "Musk's favorite tropes of video gaming and simulations," in an effort to showcase "the dangers of becoming like the 'Game Master' in Ready Player One."
Yet the moments that are the most damning of Musk's character are when Gibney lays bare the gulf between Musk's words and reality.
In a section of the film about the safety of Tesla's full self-driving software, Gibney shows footage from a deposition in which a company engineer reveals that a promotional video claiming to show a Tesla driving fully autonomously was staged. The engineer said when the car was filmed trying to park itself, it crashed into a fence.
Even as Musk has repeatedly celebrated the self-driving technology, 65 deaths have been linked to car crashes where Tesla's software was a contributing factor, according to a public database that tracks National Highway Traffic Safety Administration reports, court records and news reports. (Tesla says its "Autopilot and Full Self-Driving Capability are intended for use with a fully attentive driver, who has their hands on the wheel and is prepared to take over at any moment.")
In February 2025, Musk bragged on X that DOGE had fed the United States Agency for International Development "into the wood chipper." Gibney speaks to the agency's former administrator, Samantha Power, who gets choked up with emotion as she explains how the closure of USAID is projected to result in more than 14 million preventable deaths. The film then cuts to heart-wrenching footage of families and children in Africa who have learned nutritional aid was being cut off.
As the repercussions of Musk's actions are tallied, Gibney keeps coming back to the same question: How does his wealth keep growing despite it all?
Lawrence Fossi, a longtime critic of Musk and Tesla, appears on screen to offer an explanation: investing in Musk's companies is not a bet on corporate America, "it's investing in a religion."
This observation gets to the heart of Gibney's central argument about Musk: that he is a hype artist whose highest skill is making financiers and the public believe in him.
"His motives may have been pure at the beginning. But over time, in an attempt to get his companies to succeed, he ruthlessly broke the rules many of us live by. Musk is just the latest example of what I call noble cause corruption. Essentially, it's a belief that you're justified in breaking the rules because you think you are a force for good. Over time, as you begin to imagine you can get away with anything, the corruption becomes as total as the zealotry," Gibney said in promotional materials provided to the press.
Ashley St. Clair, formerly a pro-Trump influencer who has turned against the MAGA movement, plays a major role in the film. She's Musk's ex and the mother of one of his children.
In the film, St. Clair says one of the more outlandish and confounding claims Musk made to her was that he would "unleash the anomaly in the matrix" ahead of the 2024 presidential election to ensure Donald Trump would win. She said Musk texted her that he has "over 10 thousand lasers in space." (NPR obtained and authenticated the texts between Musk and St. Clair.)
Gibney asked St. Clair if she understood this to be a reference to Musk's SpaceX. St. Clair replied, "I don't know where else he has lasers," before dwelling on the moment, as if to force the viewer to think hard about Musk's sci-fi gibberish.
Election officials repeatedly debunked the false narrative purporting to show a connection between SpaceX's Starlink satellites and the November vote count. Nonetheless, the theory ricocheted online in the days after the 2024 election.
Musk's legal threat to Gibney seized on that moment with St. Clair, saying the film elevating a disproven theory is problematic. Musk's lawyer wrote that "the insinuation is false" and "the material refuting it is public."
While most of Gibney's film is rooted in solid facts, he does dabble in conspiratorial thinking in the scene about the "lasers in space," and later in the film when he raises the specter of Musk using DOGE data to somehow interfere in the November midterms, another idea without any evidence.
Throughout the film, other Musk texts emerge.
After The Wall Street Journal published an article detailing Musk's alleged recreational drug use, which was raising concerns among leaders at SpaceX, St. Claire said Musk personally called News Corp. owner Rupert Murdoch in hopes he would intervene to stop the reporting. He did not.
Musk then texted St. Clair that the Journal's articles were "saying that I'm high all the time."
Musk added in a separate text: "I mean, I'm high a little … sure," punctuating the message with a shrugging emoji.
results.summary:
Oscar-winning director Alex Gibney explores the life and influence of Elon Musk in his new documentary, *Musk*, which examines the billionaire's business practices and political impact.

### Key Points
- The documentary, which runs three hours and 45 minutes, is scheduled for a theatrical release on October 16.
- Gibney features interviews with Musk’s father, former partners, and business associates to analyze the tech mogul's rise and controversial management style.
- The film highlights the Department of Government Efficiency (DOGE) and Musk’s influence on the 2024 presidential election and federal policy.
- Evidence presented includes a deposition regarding staged Tesla self-driving footage and reports linking Tesla software to 65 fatal crashes.
- The production utilizes an AI-generated avatar of Musk to narrate his own past statements, a stylistic choice that has drawn criticism for its distracting nature.

### Why it Matters
The film frames Musk as a "confidence man" whose immense wealth and power rely on market hype and the erosion of traditional corporate boundaries. By documenting his transition from a tech entrepreneur to a central figure in federal governance, the project raises critical questions about the risks of unchecked influence in the modern era.

results.title: Future of Marketing Briefing: One more helping, for gluttons still hungry for Publicis and PepsiCo takes
results.author: Seb Joseph
results.content:
This Future of Marketing Briefing covers the latest in marketing for Digiday+ members and is distributed over email every Friday at 10 a.m. ET. More from the series →
Yes, more thoughts on what it means, or doesn’t, that Publicis walked away from competing for Coca-Cola’s media dollars to grab PepsiCo’s instead. But in my defense, it felt right to wait until the hot takes, livestreams and articles on the fallout died down a bit. If you’ve got the stomach for more, read on for where the industry stands on this.
Publicis is in its imperialist era
It’s been known for a while that Publicis was operating on a different level to its rivals but the decision is arguably the clearest articulation of that so far. If PepsiCo were a mid-tier account, skipping the pitch would just be a client taking a shortcut. In reality, however, it’s one of the largest — worth around $1.7 billion. At this size, on a rival scale to Coca-Cola, no pitch means the market’s two biggest advertisers both gave serious thought to handing Publicis this kind of money. One did, on trust alone.
“I’ve been on billion dollar pitches and they’re one of the most painful experiences on earth for agency execs,” said Patrick Ryan, a former Omnicom exec, who now runs 300, a specialist growth consultancy for agencies. “The ability to be able to do what Publicis did without a pitch is impressive because the cost savings (both money and people) there are absolutely vast.”
Every rival network watching this wants its own version of the story — the account that arrives without a fight because the client was sold on the pitch hook, line and sinker. But wanting it doesn’t make it happen. Holdco bosses have to earn that kind of trust themselves, and that’s less about how many capabilities they have to offer and more about how convincingly they get knitted together. Publicis has cleared that bar in a way nobody else currently has, to the point where it may not need to pitch for the accounts that matter most. Microsoft already moved its estimated $700 million global media planning and buying business from Dentsu to Publicis earlier this year. Coke did something similar a year ago when it gave Publicis its ad dollars in North America. Add the six major pitches Publicis CEO Arthur Sadoun said the group walked from in the first half of the year, and neither number would be surprising to see climb further before December. This is Publicis’ imperialist era.
Being imperial also means being pragmatic
The deal reads as opportunistic on its face. But that framing undersells the calculation Sadoun and his team clearly ran before committing to it. After all, Coca-Cola was an account he had coveted for years, going so far as to win its massive North American media and data business from WPP last year. Going head-to-head with the British holding company in a fierce, two-horse global shootout earlier this year put Sadoun about as close to capturing the crown jewel as he had ever been. Walking away from the MediaSense-managed pitch at that exact moment takes some explaining.
So here goes: the closer Publicis got, the clearer it would have become that the global business came with operational strings it couldn’t easily cut. Following Coca-Cola’s massive agency overhaul in 2021, WPP became the beverage giant’s primary global marketing partner. To handle that vast remit, WPP built — and continues to operate — OpenX, an entirely bespoke agency and operating system hardwired directly into Coca-Cola’s infrastructure.
Because WPP still controls the vast majority of Coca-Cola’s global creative work, production studios, and digital asset libraries, they retain a structural lock on the client’s day-to-day operations. Had Publicis won the global media dollars under that model, its own unified tech stack would have spent years awkwardly plugging into and chafing against a rival network’s underlying software. That friction is especially hard to swallow when it compromises the highest-margin facets of modern agency revenue: data orchestration, platform licensing, and software-as-a-service fees wired directly around a client’s first-party data.
Control was always the real prize
If billings were the whole story, walking from Coca-Cola for a net gain of roughly $400 million makes no sense. Here’s why: Publicis already held around $600 million of PepsiCo’s business through an Asia-Pacific win 18 months earlier, so that portion isn’t new revenue, it’s already on the books. Subtract that from PepsiCo’s core global media spend of roughly $1.8 billion, per ComVergence, and the genuinely new business comes to about $1.2 billion. Sodastream adds another $150 to $200 million to the wider PepsiCo relationship, but sits outside that core calculation. Against the $1.2 billion, Publicis is giving up the $800 million Coca-Cola North America account it won from WPP only a year ago as part of the same move. Net the two out and the real gain lads around $400 million — a fraction of the $1.7 billion headline attached to this deal.
Which is to say this was never about media dollars. It was about control, instead. By bundling media, identity and technology under a unified mandate, PepsiCo hands Publicis complete ownership of the platform layer — the data orchestration, the proprietary SaaS tooling and the high-margin enterprise fees that a standard media buying commission never captures. Coca-Cola’s Open X system was structurally designed to withstand that lucrative software layer from outside agencies. By walking away from Coke to accept a smaller headline number on paper, Publicis revealed what it actually values: the uncompromised control of a client’s digital infrastructure.
At this level, relationships are key
Of course, capabilities matter and knitting them together matters even moreso. But none of it is enough on its own to push a CMO to turn its back on a holdco without a pitch — let alone one it’s stuck with for more than 25 years. That part comes down to people.
Jane Wakely, evp, chief consumer and marketing officer and chief growth officer, worked with Publicis in a previous role at Mars. She didn’t need a capabilities deck to know what Publicis could deliver, she’d already watched it happen. That kind of trust can’t be matched by a rival’s tech stack or undercutting on price. It’s built over years, in a different job, on a different account, long before PepsiCo’s business was ever in place. Which is presumably why it only took one capabilities meeting, according to a source with knowledge of it, to decide the holdco was up to the job.
It also wasn’t a call Wakely got to make quietly. Putting a 25-year incumbent up for replacement without a pitch meant making that case internally, to a CFO who’d want to know what was actually being bought and to a CEO who’d want to know why the safer, more conventional route wasn’t good enough. Wakely staked her own reputation on the answer being Publicis, with no competitive process to point to if it went wrong.
No, this isn’t a sign of the times
The pitch isn’t going the way of the dodo anytime soon. It’s too important strategically and commercially for most CMOs and their procurement teams to walk away from. What’s changing is who gets to skip it. Trust built over years — the kind Wakely brought over from Mars — buys an exemption most CMOs don’t have in their agencies. Without it, the pitch is the only mechanism that justifies a decision this size to a CFO who wasn’t in the room when the relationship was built.
A door closes for Omnicom, as another opens
Omnicom’s exposure here goes beyond a number on the balance sheet. On a net revenue basis, Omnicom runs a healthy adjusted EDITDA margin, comfortably enough to absorb a $400 million revenue loss without much financial drama. What’s harder to absorb is the question it raises everywhere else.
PepsiCo was Omnicom’s account for more than 25 years — exactly the kind of relationship the American holdco built its reputation on retaining. Apple, Renault-Nissan and McDonald’s sit in the same bracket, decades-long deals that have never gone through a competitive review. None of those clients needed a reason to ask questions before. They have one now, whatever the eventual answer turns out to be.
But there’s an opening too. With Publicis stepping back from Coca-Cola’s global revenue, Omnicom becomes a credible contender for business it wasn’t seriously competing for a month ago. Whether that logic appeals to Coke as much as it does to Omnicom is a different question, and that won’t resolve for a while yet.
What we’ve heard
“I would say it is early days there [on invoicing clients for token costs]. There is not much of that yet. There is not actually much of a meaningful increase in token cost overall at the business. There is some. It is something that we certainly are discussing in meetings on a regular basis to come up with a model that makes sense for us and for our clients and the process and controls that we need in place to manage those token costs and then to measure them. To get reimbursed for the additional cost to deliver what we do, there are a number of moving costs in that model. Ultimately, we are going to move towards a more output-driven model from a revenue perspective. We think that will be a long-term positive in the end.”
— Omnicom CFO Phil Angelastro said at the Goldman Sachs’ Communacopia + Technology Conference
Numbers to know
34%: Percentage of U.S. shoppers that navigate retailer websites primarily via search
$820: JPMorgan’s new price target for Meta shares, up from $640, after the launch of its Muse AI agent
October 30th: The date from which Google is opening personalized ad targeting to alcohol brands on YouTube
100: The number of creators that the U.S. Open approved this year
What we’ve covered
Amazon’s advertisers can now buy ads inside ChatGPT, in a U.S. pilot starting today with Delta Vacations among the first. It’s the latest in Amazon’s run of premium supply deals, and a big partner for OpenAI’s still-immature ad business.
The FTC says Amazon secretly inflated ad prices through its auction, but ad buyers are barely reacting because opaque auctions are already the norm across Google, Meta and programmatic. As long as performance holds up, advertisers mostly don’t care.
Bots and AI agents now make up over half of web traffic. Some brands welcome it because AI-referred shoppers convert well, but others find it’s corrupting retargeting and pushing budgets towards social, retail media and first party data.
Heading into the fourth quarter of 2026, creators are moving into Hollywood and the c-suite, brands are turning staff into creators, and diversifying income matters more than ever.
What we’re reading
Serp Api has countersued Reddit on antitrust grounds, alleging that since mid-2024 it let only Google crawl the site under a reported $60 million-a-year deal while blocking Bing, DuckDuckGo, and others, according to PPC Land. It argues Reddit is charging for content its users actually own, and that the lockout came six months before the anti-scraping protection Reddit now cites.
The U.S. Open roughly doubled its accredited creators to about 100 this year, and a group filming loudly during Naomi Osaka’s match forced the umpire to stop play. Players like Jessica Pegula called it disrespectful, sparking calls for creators to be briefed on tennis etiquette, per Fast Company.
Australia has proposed a “digital duty of care” law that would force social platforms to let users switch off algorithmic recommendations and see only accounts they follow, building on its under-16s ban, per Financial Times. It would also require protections for under-18s across games, apps and AI chatbots, with fines of up to A$109.2 million for breaches.
JPMorgan has upgraded Meta to overweight on the strength of its new Muse AI agent, which hit number three in the U.S. App Store, raising its price target to $820. It’s a sign Wall Street is warming to Meta’s AI strategy after a year of scepticism left the stock lagging the Nasdaq, per Bloomberg.
Retail giants like Walmart, Kroger and Amazon have launched AI assistants allowing consumers to ask for recommendations or curated shopping lists. Now, Instacart has made it easier for other retailers such as regional grocers to follow in their footsteps.
AI is changing agency work. Agencies are adding provisions to existing contracts instead of rewriting their MSAs.
The FTC’s Amazon charges presage Google’s second antitrust let-off in a year, while The Trade Desk sheds hundreds.

Publicis Groupe has secured a major partnership with PepsiCo by prioritizing control over digital infrastructure, effectively walking away from competing for Coca-Cola’s global media business to ensure operational autonomy.

### Key Points
- Publicis prioritized PepsiCo’s account to gain full control over data orchestration and proprietary software-as-a-service (SaaS) tooling.
- The deal represents a net revenue gain of approximately $400 million, as Publicis relinquished its existing $800 million North American contract with Coca-Cola.
- PepsiCo’s decision to bypass a competitive pitch was driven by the long-standing professional trust between CMO Jane Wakely and Publicis leadership.
- Coca-Cola’s existing "OpenX" operating system, managed by WPP, created structural friction that would have limited Publicis’ ability to integrate its own tech stack.
- Omnicom lost the PepsiCo account after a 25-year tenure, signaling a shift in how major advertisers evaluate agency partnerships and long-term vendor relationships.

### Why it Matters
This move highlights a strategic shift where top-tier agencies prioritize the integration of proprietary technology and data control over simple media-buying billings. By securing uncompromised access to a client's digital infrastructure, Publicis is positioning itself to capture higher-margin revenue streams that traditional agency models often miss.

results.title: The Tim Ferriss Show Transcripts: Why Kids Can Learn 10x Faster Than We Think — Niels Hoven of Mentava (Tim Coaching Session) (#882)
results.author: Tim Ferriss
results.content:
Please enjoy this live, unscripted working session with a founder, one of only two I’ve done this year. Niels Hoven (@NielsHoven) is the founder and CEO of Mentava, a company building software to support fast learners.
Additional podcast platforms
Listen to this episode on Apple Podcasts, Spotify, Overcast, Podcast Addict, Pocket Casts, Castbox, YouTube Music, Amazon Music, Audible, or on your favorite podcast platform.
Transcripts may contain a few typos. With many episodes lasting 2+ hours, it can be difficult to catch minor errors. Enjoy!
Tim Ferriss: Niels, it’s nice to see you. Thanks for making the time. Looking forward to this.
Niels Hoven: Thanks so much. I appreciate the chance to be here.
Tim Ferriss: Absolutely. And it was fun for me to take a trip down memory lane in a sense, because I remember exactly where I was when we first had our very initial long conversation about Mentava and I got super amped. I was in British Columbia walking around a friend’s cabin. I remember exactly right next to a river, freezing cold outside, snow on the ground. And digging back into the website, looking at the testimonials, watching some of the videos of kids, I was like, “Yes, I remember very clearly why I invested so long ago.” It feels like ages ago. It was quite a while back. And we will get to the bio. I actually want to use part of this working session to go through the bio as I have it here intended for me to read, because I think the wordsmithing may apply to other places, including the website, including potentially paid acquisition.
But before we get to that, why don’t you—let’s hear it from your mouth. What is Mentava? What is the latest draft of your quick explanation of what Mentava is?
Niels Hoven: All right. The latest draft is that Mentava is software that is designed to let kids learn as fast as they’re capable of learning instead of just at the pace assigned to their age. And the first product we have is our early literacy software, which is designed for kids, preschoolers, as young as generally three to get to a second-grade reading level.
Tim Ferriss: And what is a second-grade reading level? Let’s just say I’m a first-time parent. I don’t know what it means. What is an eager to learn, reasonably smart second-grader doing with their reading by the end of second grade?
Niels Hoven: Our finish line is basically able to read easy reader books on your own. So think Green Eggs and Ham, Hop on Pop, the Elephant & Piggie series, the conscious competence level of being able to read.
Tim Ferriss: Okay, got it. And what are some stories? And I recognize these are not RCTs, right? So for the people out there who are going to try to needle everything, a lot of these are anecdotal of course, but you also have data in terms of performance on the app, right? It’s not just a subjective measurement, but could you just give some stories related to kids learning to read faster than one might expect?
Niels Hoven: Right. We had a set of two-year-old twins who were reading Hop on Pop, Green Eggs and Ham, these early reader books before their third birthday. We have a three-year-old who—
Tim Ferriss: That’s the [inaudible] that I saw where they were standing.
Niels Hoven: Oh yeah, you just retweeted that video.
Tim Ferriss: Yeah. The parents were projecting the game onto some large screen and the two twins were basically just playing and competing with each other to read. Wild. They were so excited to read.
Niels Hoven: It is really adorable. It’s funny, there’s so much fear around, but if I give my kid these academic opportunities when they’re so young, are they going to stress out? Are they going to freak out? But no, it’s actually fun. Kids are these little sponges. They want to learn everything.
Tim Ferriss: And just as background, well, why don’t you tell one or two more stories and then I want to hear how Mentava came to be, not the Iliad version, like the abbreviated version, but maybe you can give a few more examples because people might say, “Okay, fine. You got the Wonder Twins, but we need more than the Wonder Twins.” So what else have you seen?
Niels Hoven: We had a three-year-old who learned to read in about three months. We had a kindergartner who was behind and his mom asked us, “Can we use this software to help him catch up?” And she came back to me a little later and said, “Yeah, he’s reading now. The teacher says she’s never seen a kid catch up so fast.” What was the phrasing? She was like, “The teacher didn’t actually say this, but I could read between the lines. I could tell that the teacher really wanted to say your kid was just a terrible reader.” The teacher didn’t say that. The parent was like, “But I could read between the lines. I knew what she wanted to say.” And the teacher said she’d never seen anyone catch up that fast.
And the thing that actually really stuck with me from that one was the mom was saying the kid used to come to her and tell her, “Hey mom, there’s this kid in my class who’s so smart. He’s able to read and do all these things.” And then she said, “He came back to me the other day and said, ‘Mom, I can read like he can read now.’”
Tim Ferriss: That’s so cool.
Niels Hoven: That was just really neat.
Tim Ferriss: I was watching the two-minute, maybe three-minute demo. I’m not sure. It’s pretty short. I don’t think you guys publicize or use it much, but the demo video that you sent over.
Niels Hoven: It’s a terrible demo, but yeah, it’s out there.
Tim Ferriss: It’s terrible except there is one slide, let’s call it, it’s text that is a testimonial that is kind of below the fold on laptop on your love letters section with all these parents sharing their experiences, which is roughly more progress in one week with my daughter than in roughly six months of kindergarten. And that’s bananas, but it’s not so bananas as to be outside of the realm of possibility. And you become somewhat of an adept in the sport of sparring with critics on X, the artist formerly known as Twitter. And we may chat about that, to what extent it’s helpful to engage in or even provoke the culture wars. But I have seen a few. I think there’s one notable. You’re good at responding to the critics in a way that gets people to sign up for Mentava. And there was someone who said like, “The learning process, I have a four-year degree that was earned because learning is complex and you cannot simplify it and we’re not focused on outcomes. We’re focused on all this hand wavy stuff.” And certainly—
Niels Hoven: This was an educator who said something like, “You will never convince me that results are the driver of education. You’ll never convince me that efficacy is supposed to be one of our goals.”
Tim Ferriss: People can watch the documentary Waiting for “Superman” if they want to see the part of the sorry state of things. But I was introduced to you. How was I introduced to you? It was Eric Ries, I believe, of The Lean Startup.
Niels Hoven: Also one of our investors.
Tim Ferriss: Also one of your investors because I think he knew or intuited that I’m very much on the same page. You can learn things much, you meaning adults, but also humans, broadly speaking, can learn things much, much, much more quickly than conventional wisdom would suggest. And I could go off on this long list of things, but how do you do it? How do you do it? How did Mentava come to be, short version, and why does it work? How and why does it work?
Niels Hoven: Short version of how it came to be. Mentava started during the pandemic. At the time, my wife and I, we had three little kids, so we both have full-time jobs. We’re locked down in this 600-square-foot, one-bedroom apartment. My kids want to learn. They’re young kids. They’re these little sponges. They want to learn to read. They want to do math, but I have a full-time job. I don’t have time to teach them and be their teacher every step of the way. What I really want is I want them to be able to teach themselves, which aside from just being practical in that situation is just this life skill that I feel is really, really important. And so, I started looking around for software or apps that could support my kids as they’re learning, and there just wasn’t very much out there. I found a couple of things that were okay and we made it work, and it was honestly surprising how well they were able to learn despite using software that really wasn’t designed for having kids teach themselves.
And so, other parents noticed what I was doing. They asked me questions about it. I pointed them to the same software, and some of them had some success and some of them didn’t. And really what I realized as all of this was going on was that the problem was in the design of the software. No one is designing software for three and four-year-olds to be learning on their own. It’s not that it’s impossible, it’s just that it’s really, really hard. But my background is in games. I spent a long time designing games and designing tutorials, and it’s just design problems all the way down. I felt like this is a problem that I could solve, that I wanted to solve for myself, that I wanted to solve for other people, and that’s where Mentava came from.
Tim Ferriss: And what’s the magic sauce? Why does it work? Why is it better than the 12 other things that I’ve seen you rate from a scale of, I think, 1 to 10 in different ways and giving your reasons?
Niels Hoven: Right. I think the key things that Mentava brings to the table is an extremely optimized curriculum and a lot of really good motivation design. I think the curriculum advantage should not be as much of an advantage as it is because reading and math are both basically solved problems. We know how to teach reading. You teach kids letter sounds and then you teach them to blend them together. And honestly, for $15, you can get a book off of Amazon that will let you do that. You have to be the teacher. It’s a lot of heavy lifting from the parents’ side, but it will get the job done. So it’s kind of unconscionable that this has been a debate in education for a generation, but this is very much a solved problem. So we take phonics, we optimize it, we teach it really nicely. We make really good UX. We make it really easy for two, three, and four-year-olds to use.
Tim Ferriss: And this is on, typically, a tablet?
Niels Hoven: Yeah, on an iPad, just as an anecdote is where the bar is hanging in terms of low hang design. In one of the apps that I was using before we built Mentava to have my kids learn, if you have a two-year-old, if you have a three-year-old and they’re using an iPad, they kind of brace it on their belly and they hold it there while they’re tapping away at it. And a very common situation that happens is their little tubby toddler belly hangs over the edge of the iPad and you get all these extraneous touches at the bottom of the iPad. And in one of the apps that we were using, every time that happened, the app would crash. It was just a tap. So you have this—
Tim Ferriss: Belly crash.
Niels Hoven: —two-year-old toddler belly constantly crashing the app. And so we take into account all these little things where you have a kid who doesn’t know how to read trying to use these educational apps. The other piece that we really bring to the table is motivation. I think there’s a lot of people really don’t understand how sophisticated motivation design is. But if you look at video games, if you walk into a casino and you walk through the slot machine aisles, human motivation is kind of a solved problem. We know how to get people to do the things that we want them to do over and over and kind of, I don’t know exactly how to say that.
Tim Ferriss: You mean like variable reward or how does the slot machine example map to motivation design?
Niels Hoven: Right. The slot machine example is probably the crudest example. It’s the easiest way to motivate someone because the metaphor for motivation that I like to use is it’s like trying to get someone to jump through a hoop. And so, you can either increase the size of the reward on the other side or you can lower the hoop. And so, slot machines are kind of the purest example of this where they dangle the biggest reward you could possibly imagine, which is like a million dollar jackpot, and they’ve moved the hoop as low as you possibly can, which is just press this button over and over again. And so for that specific use case, it has been solved. And so our goal with Mentava is, okay, the hoop we want kids to jump through is learning all of these phonic sounds and learning to blend them together.
So how, through really good user experience design, can we lower that hoop as low as we possibly can? And then what can we dangle on the other side of that hoop to make kids want to come back and do this every single day? And for that, we use a lot of insights and design principles from game design about helping kids feel motivation, about visualizing the progress that they’ve made, about twiddling the right reward centers in the brain in just the right way that we celebrate their intrinsic motivation rather than trying to replace it extrinsically.
Tim Ferriss: So Niels, let’s move next to your bio. And if you could indulge me, which might end up seeming like a very pedantic exercise, I’m just going to go through and tell you how I would change certain words because I think we’re going to talk a lot about these magical things that allow us to produce images in brains at a distance. All words. All right. How do you pronounce your last name correctly? Remind me.
Niels Hoven: Hoven.
Tim Ferriss: Hoven. All right.
Niels Hoven: Hoven.
Tim Ferriss: Niels Hoven. On X, if you want to see front lines of the culture wars, @NielsHoven. He’s the founder and CEO of Mentava, a company building software to support unusually fast learners. This phrasing, unusually fast learners, I would actually just scrap unusually and go straight to fast learners. Part of the reason for that is that when I saw this on the website, I was like, “Well, what is unusually fast?” Even if I consider my kid fast, maybe unusually fast is what, 1 out of 100? 1 out of 1,000? And I stumbled. So I made note of things that I read twice or that I stumbled over. And this is a subjective take, but since I’m in the midst of having just recently cut an 870-page book to 350 and now I’m doing all of the fine tuning, this is how my brain is calibrated at the moment.
Okay. So software to support unusually fast learners or support fast learners. High achieving kids are dramatically underserved by today’s education system. I would also, I think high achieving for me at least, I think about pegging to letter grades in high school or college. I might just replace that or you could scrap high achieving. When in doubt, take it out is another writing dictum. So it’s like kids, high achieving kids, eager kids maybe, right?
Niels Hoven: Oh yeah. Okay.
Tim Ferriss: Eager kids are dramatically underserved by today’s education system. And again, I recognize this might be a little laborious for a second, but it’s going to tie into things that come up later. Okay. Niels created Mentava to allow top performing students to achieve their potential. I think we can scrap top performing also, students to achieve their potential. Great. Now I would actually scrap this entire second paragraph, which I’ll explain in a moment, but while most education companies focus on raising the floor, Mentava’s mission is to remove the ceiling. I have very strong opinions about this. I know it’s on the website. I get the turn of phrase and I understand why there’s a degree of clever wordsmithing here. I don’t like this as a positioning for you because what I ended up stumbling over here, I was like, raising the floor, remove the ceiling, remove the ceiling. I guess that’s as high as the best performing students.
So raising the floor, does that mean accommodating and helping the lowest performing students? I ended up dissecting it and just spending a lot of time thinking about it. So I’ve read that line a lot, but let’s move on. Is my understanding of that correct? Am I actually understanding that sense as it’s intended?
Niels Hoven: Yeah, basically you are. I think one of the challenges we are struggling with is how we kind of target what we see as more of a niche audience that deeply values education, is willing to pay for it and has kids that are being unsupported academically. And so we’ve been playing with different turns of phrases to try and speak to these people, but I agree. I don’t think we’ve found the right one yet.
Tim Ferriss: Yeah. I would also say, I think it’s a big niche, frankly, which you may have already concluded, but their early literacy software, meaning Mentava’s early literacy software for preschoolers is used and trusted by some of the most influential people in the world. Don’t love that. We can come back to that just because it’s something that anyone could claim unless you have things to point to, right? And maybe you do. We can come back to that. Mentava blends careful curriculum design with best in class motivation design. I think, for instance, we are not that far from the beginning of the new year. I think doubling down on motivation design if you’re going to do more X posts around January would actually be very interesting and do some very interesting things there that would drive conversions, but developed through years of experience building mobile and I’m guessing the way you pronounce this is AAA games.
I don’t actually know what AAA games are, but that sounds like a good thing and I have heard it before. This is, I think, the money shot in some respects. Prior to Mentava, Niels worked at Cloudflare, ClassDojo, and Pocket Gems where he ran the highest grossing mobile game in the world in 2011. That says you know what you’re doing very, very clearly. So I would be inclined to scrap that whole second paragraph and then move up the third. And then it goes to mentava.com and it has all the links and everything else. So M-E-N-T-A-V-A, if people are wondering. But I don’t want to belabor the intro, but we are going to spend a lot of time on messaging.
And you very kindly sent a skeleton framework that we could use for going into the conversation. I think we already checked off kids can learn much faster than people think. Problem two, I think, is maybe not immediately obvious to folks, but the problem, and if you don’t mind, I’ll just read it. We waste the low pressure elementary school years and then pour on pressure in high school. And it’s like, okay, maybe I agree with that. Okay, waste low pressure. How should we capitalize on low pressure and are we accidentally turning it into high pressure if we add something like this? I mean, looking at the kids playing it, at least the video I’ve seen, it wouldn’t seem that way. I do like, I know I’m kind of spoiling the delivery by offering the punchline, but if you don’t mind.
Niels Hoven: Yeah, go for it.
Tim Ferriss: So you had two, right? You had two sub-bullets under that. Schools actively slow down fast learners. Yes, 100% agree. They wouldn’t let my son learn algebra, et cetera. Is that your son, your actual son?
Niels Hoven: My son, yep.
Tim Ferriss: Yeah. Okay. Early acceleration means less pressure later. That I think is super, super, super interesting as a point that could be really used, maybe not in exactly that form. And then number three solution. Mentava lets kids accelerate without requiring parents to become teachers or taskmasters. And that’s through, as you pointed out, the very finely tuned curriculum and motivation design. And I would agree that schools are surprisingly bad at both.
Tim Ferriss: So what are some of the current challenges? How would you lay out the hierarchy of problems to solve, opportunities to capitalize on, however you would like to phrase it or list it out? Where should we go next?
Niels Hoven: Zooming way out. We’ve built a product that we are really proud of that when our customers use it, they rave about it and they tell their friends about it. I think we have not figured out. We are really good at product design and we are not so good at marketing. We are trying to explain a problem that a lot of parents don’t realize that they have, that their kids could be doing so much more, that their kids are going to be held back when they get to elementary school. By the time parents realize that they had this problem, that their kids are bored and not achieving their potential. It’s kind of too late to—or the biggest opportunities to do something about it are now behind them. And then for even the parents who are looking for a product in this space that can help support their kids’ learning, they’re not experts.
And what differentiates our software from a lot of the other stuff out there is really nuanced. And so, how do we differentiate what we feel is a premium product when the differentiates is really nuanced and in thousands of small decisions that customers can’t look at themselves? It’s kind of like trying to explain what makes this video game better than this other video game. It’s a very hard thing to explain or has been for us.
Tim Ferriss: Right. It’s a thousand decisions that add up to a very distinct feeling maybe on some level. Okay.
Niels Hoven: We found a lot of the parents who came to us immediately sort of already feel this problem intensely because sometimes it’s immigrants who come to the US and then are just shocked at how much worse the education system is here than what they experienced. So they just see this immediately and they’re like, “I am not going to have any part of this. Niels Hoven: Yeah. You—

results.title: How Meta tried, and failed, to grab its employees' data for AI
results.author: Charles Rollet
results.content:
This spring, members of Meta's elite AI unit, TBD, decided that the social media giant needed an edge in the AI race. The edge they were looking for? Data from tens of thousands of Meta employees.
Meta introduced a program to collect data from employees for AI training, called Model Capability Initiative (MCI). Employees' keystrokes and mouse movements could help Meta's AI replicate how humans use computers, a critical task as AI labs race to automate white-collar work like coding and accounting.
But Meta had a very human problem: its own employees, who revolted over the mandatory project as soon as it was announced. Their resistance took the form of flyers, memes, and a viral petition against what some characterized as "the Eye of Sauron." Organizers say that their constant pressure forced Meta to make concessions and eventually drop the program.
Corporate data has become a gold mine for training AI because it helps algorithms deal with messy, real-world work environments — and workers are increasingly fighting back. Former Spirit Airlines flight attendants temporarily blocked Google from buying the bankrupt airline's database for $10 million. Over 1,800 Meta employees signed a petition calling for the company's internal tracking to be stopped.
Meta halted the tracking program after an internal data leak this summer, saying it would switch to being opt-in only. Two months later, Meta says the program remains suspended. The company declined to comment further for this article.
This story is part of a new series called The AI Data Grab, examining how companies are racing to collect as much data as possible to build the world's most advanced AI systems. For this story, Business Insider interviewed half a dozen current and former Meta employees, and reviewed internal posts and other materials to uncover new details about how the program began, how workers fought it, and the leak that brought it to a halt.
How Meta began its MCI program
The MCI program originated within Meta's AI unit, called TBD, a group of about 100 researchers widely considered the tip of the spear of the tech giant's AI efforts.
One of the leaders of the effort was Rylan Schaeffer, three people told Business Insider. Schaeffer reported to two people at the apex of Meta's AI efforts: its AI chief, Alexandr Wang, and a top researcher, Jack Rae. According to his LinkedIn, Schaeffer left Meta in July to work on something new. He didn't respond to requests for comment from Business Insider.
TBD members rarely interact with Meta's legions of other employees, working in a separate area within Meta's Menlo Park campus, according to two people familiar with the matter. Their online workplace profiles are sparse, displaying few details beyond their name — unlike more typical profiles, which showcase people's managers and what they're working on.
One April morning, Meta announced the MCI program to the wider workforce.
"While AI models excel at research and technical skills like coding, they still lack some of the basic ways that humans use computers like choosing from dropdowns and keyboard shortcuts," an internal announcement read.
The announcement drew an immediate backlash and a slew of angry-face emojis after Meta's chief technology officer, Andrew Bosworth, said there would be no opting out.
"This makes me super uncomfortable" was the top-rated comment in response to the announcement.
Bosworth would become a lightning rod inside Meta for his staunch defense of MCI.
He touted its strict privacy guardrails after a cybersecurity engineer asked how Meta would secure the data the program collects and accused the AI division of "moving fast and implementing security as an afterthought."
Bosworth replied, "That isn't remotely a fair characterization! How would any of this end up in 'the open'? This is tightly controlled data."
Meta employees fight the 'Eye of Sauron'
The intense online backlash spurred a grassroots movement from Meta employees. Workers feared MCI would capture sensitive data that US workers plugged into their laptops, such as passwords, immigration forms, and credit card numbers, two organizers told Business Insider.
Some workers said they also feared that the screen capture data would be used to replace scores of Meta employees with AI — a risk many hadn't taken that seriously before, a third organizer said, calling it a "big reality check."
Employees posted anti-AI memes in an internal Meta employee channel. One meme seen by Business Insider portrayed Meta's management as the omniscient villain, Christof, from "The Truman Show." Employees jokingly dubbed the icon that appeared whenever MCI recorded their screens "the Eye of Sauron."
An anti-MCI petition gained steam, garnering over 1,800 signatures. Staffers spelled out the link to the MCI petition on a building at Meta's Burlingame office.
A small group of activists within Meta spread flyers around campuses, making sure they included language from the National Labor Relations Act that speaking out against workplace issues is protected, one of the organizers said.
In what the activists viewed as an early concession, Meta allowed employees to temporarily opt out of the tracking program for up to 30 minutes in June, during which they could perform more sensitive tasks they didn't want ingested by an AI model.
It wasn't enough for Meta's anti-MCI activists, who called it "insufficient and unsatisfactory" in a statement to Business Insider at the time.
"We demand, and will continue to demand, that Mark and his leadership team scrap MCI entirely, immediately, forever," they wrote, referring to Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg.
Soon, Meta's own security decisions would force its leadership to take drastic action.
'Hey Metamate, define the word 'hubris' for me'
In late June, Meta engineers woke up to an internal post that had gone viral among employees. An engineer had discovered that data collected by MCI had been viewable across the entire company all along, including full private conversations.
In an internal post, one employee wrote they were "incensed" that the scenario that some had warned about had come to pass. Their post was titled "MCI Data: Not So Tightly Controlled" and screenshotted Bosworth's earlier comment defending MCI's security.
"Hey Metamate, define the word 'hubris' for me," another employee commented, referring to Meta's internal AI assistant.
"I swear we're probably the richest yet most incompetent company to exist in tech right now," another chimed in.
Within hours, Meta turned off MCI. It told Business Insider that it suspended — but not outright canceled — the program and that, going forward, it would be optional.
Whether the data proved useful is another question. In a July Q&A with executives, a Meta manager said it had not been used to train its latest AI models, according to another person familiar with the matter. At a July town hall, Bosworth said the data was more useful than Meta thought it would be, according to two people familiar with the matter. Meta declined to comment on how, and if, the data was used.
Companies may think twice about harvesting employee data
Bosworth has made his position clear: MCI opponents didn't improve Meta.
"They made the entire company worse," he said — three times — in a leaked July audio recording published by the activist group More Perfect Union.
"I think the people who put up that petition on MCI thought they were helping. They weren't helping; they made it a lot harder for us to make changes internally," he said.
To the people who worked against MCI, the opposite is true. Despite mass layoffs, they came together to push back against the harvesting of their data. They say their activism forced Meta to make the program opt-in, if it's ever reintroduced.
"This would not have happened without brave acts of employee resistance," the MCI Petition website reads.
After the intense backlash from Meta employees, other companies will think twice about forcing workers to give up their data to train them, said William Fitzgerald, the founder of advocacy and communications firm The Worker Agency.
"It was a historic win," he said. "Zuckerberg wanted more data — he tried to do it this way, but it didn't work."
